And Palmeiras was no longer the only unbeaten home team in the 2026 Brasileirão. Victor Hugo — after a helping hand from Carlos Miguel — and Igor Gomes secured Atlético-MG’s 2-1 win over the competition leaders. The result was also celebrated by Flamengo, who had stumbled earlier. They had around 70% possession, and Atlético managed just one dangerous chance — which was denied by Carlos Miguel. Then came the second half and, in the ninth minute, a massive mistake. Cassierra was played in, beat his marker and took a shot. Abel Ferreira turned to two players coming back from injury: Felipe Anderson and Vitor Roque. The push for an equalizer paid off in the 75th minute, with the No. 11 showing composure and benefiting from a deflection to score. Out of favor under Eduardo Domínguez at Galo, Igor Gomes had come on in the 71st minute. He had not played since April 29. And it was he who scored Galo’s second after Cassierra got the better of Felipe Anderson. Palmeiras went all or nothing in the closing stages. But Galo held firm. And ended Palmeiras’ unbeaten home run in the BR. Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window. They will play again on Wednesday (29), when they face Vitória in Salvador. Atlético, meanwhile, reached 28 points. They opened up some breathing room over the bottom four and moved closer to the top five. title: BTS V's "stepped into the crowd" meme sparks global SNS frenzy - starnewskorea.com
content:
A meme playfully depicting BTS's V's friendly and bold personality has become a global sensation on social media. The internet phenomenon archive website "Know Your Meme" highlighted Bae's meme, "V stepped into the crowd." This meme spread on social media platforms such as TikTok and Instagram Reels through user-generated content that re-edited performance footage with subtitles. The meme began to spread widely in May when a short video of V naturally walking toward fans gathered at a concert venue during BTS's world tour was captioned "V stepped into the crowd." On May 30, a video created by an Instagram user using this meme received over 313,000 likes in just about a month and has since been used on other platforms such as TikTok. The phrase originated from a video caption posted by Vogue World's official Instagram account when V attended the Vogue World event last October. At the time, the account stated, "Tonight, V moved to the audience seats to watch the performance. Familiar with fashion shows, V appeared in a stunning outfit as if standing on the runway." Subsequently, the "V stepped into the crowd" meme spawned second-generation creations and is now being consumed by MZ generations worldwide as a way to express daily life using first-person point-of-view (POV) captions. The U.S. portal site Yahoo! explained that this trend began because V's name generates significant search volume and view counts globally, prompting social media users to insert the phrase into videos regardless of content in an effort to target algorithmic exposure. <© STARNEWS. content: Get the full live experience with the OneFootball app. Semi-automated offside made its Brasileirão debut on Saturday at Vila Belmiro, confirming Marcinho’s opener for Chapecoense against Santos in the 20th round. According to Globo.com, the system assessed Giovanni Augusto’s position on receiving the pass before he set up the goal, which was ruled onside and awarded five minutes into the second half. The CBF opted to introduce the technology during the Série A pause for the 2026 World Cup. It is available at all Série A club stadiums, and Palmeiras have also contracted it for Arena Barueri when Nubank Parque hosts shows. The setup uses about 30 mobile phones that require power and an internet connection. Genius supplies the system, which also operates in the Premier League, the Mexican league and in Belgium, with installations in 65 stadiums worldwide. Its use cuts the time needed for offside decisions by 33%, based on operations in those three leagues. If SAOT does not work, coaches, captains and the crowd are informed, then officials revert to manual VAR lines used until round 19. The league had been due to start with the tool, but activation was delayed to allow visits to every stadium. Devices record matches in 4K at 100 frames per second, creating a digital replica. title: Prime Video’s 2-Part Superhero Series Is So Good, It Officially Went Beyond the Comics - Collider
content: There have been valiant attempts to translate the characters from Marvel and DC comics to the small screen, but Prime Video has found success with telling darker, more intense superhero stories. The Boys is the flagship series that proved that compelling stories could still be told about the way that superheroes are perceived, particularly in an era where those in power are being called out for their misbehavior. The Boys started strong, but struggled to get ahead of the headlines and was ultimately weighed down by its source material; by comparison, Gen V is a superior adaptation because it was able to expand beyond Garth Ennis’ comics. Even though it has just as much body horror and superpowered action as The Boys, Gen V offers a coming-of-age story that also manages to be quite relatable. Although the notion of a superhero school is first introduced in “We Gotta Go Now,” a storyline in The Boys comics, Gen V introduces the campus of Godolkin University School of Crimefighting, in which individuals with powers are allowed to test their abilities and contend for a role within the Seven. Surprisingly, Gen V has a lot to say about the corporatization of education and the ties between major universities and powerful conglomerates; Vought International is a direct sponsor of Godolkin, which means that it has a say in what is taught and how history is written. Gen V released two seasons in between new installments of The Boys, but it feels like a more complete series now that both shows are concluded. The most notable idea of The Boys is that superheroes are essentially celebrities who are bought and paid for by corporations with government ties, meaning that their fandoms are being swayed for political causes. Gen V is an appropriate story for the era of superhero dominance because all the characters have some sort of power, meaning that they feel less unique. A common issue among young people is the feeling of hopelessness and inability to change world events, which is a prevailing idea throughout Gen V. There is obviously only a select number of students that can advance to a prominent placement within Vought, and it's made abundantly clear that those who don’t make it are expendable. Even though the violence and gore in Gen V is over-the-top, it’s nonetheless disturbing to see the dangerous circumstances that young people are under. What’s even more disturbing is that they are required to keep attending classes when life-and-death stakes exist, an idea that feels even more relevant for young people who grew up during the pandemic. A dark turn for the superhero series as it morphs into the very thing it mocked... Gen V strengthens The Boys because it takes place on the edges of the universe and can explore the effects of Vought's propaganda more naturally. Although there are various cameos from members of the Seven, Gen V tells a more focused story that doesn’t have to toggle between the government, the vigilantes, the superheroes, and the public. Godolkin itself is a microcosm of the world in which the characters watch their classmates get unwittingly radicalized and turned into soldiers. While it has a direct tie to The Boys (especially since several Gen V characters show up in the final season), there’s enough context about the worldbuilding that it doesn’t require the viewer to have caught up with both shows. There’s also an element of surprise that makes Gen V more exciting; there was so much speculation about how closely The Boys would follow the comic that the final season had to contend with different expectations, whereas Gen V had the freedom to chart out unwritten territory. Gen V is not only a stylistic showcase that finds new and inventive ways to express superhero powers, but also features a great collection of performances, with Jaz Sinclair as Marie Moreau being a standout. Marie’s backstory is brutally explained in the pilot episode, signifying how the development of powers is intended to be a metaphor for the process of self-discovery that adolescents go through. While The Boys has some of the most memorable villains in television history, Gen V features an impressive rogue’s gallery that got a major expansion in the second season when Hamish Linklater joined the cast as Doug Brightball, the new dean of Godolkin. It’s terrifying for a villain to be so well-integrated into a position of influence, and Linklater does a great job of finding a balance between being charismatic and creepy. Gen V was sadly cancelled at the end of its second season, but the show offers a complete story that tracks its protagonists throughout their journey into becoming adults and stepping beyond campus life. Although it's interwoven into the ending of The Boys, Gen V is satisfying because it didn't have to fulfill the same plot expectations. There was certainly an opportunity to follow these characters in subsequent adventures beyond Godolkin, but there is something powerful about expressing the uncertainty of fate in such an honest way. Prime Video has multiple spin-offs of The Boys in the works, and there will likely be more stories in this universe told in the next several years. That said, Gen V isn’t just a spin-off, but a new perspective on the material that also feels like a maturation. We want to hear from you. title: Mayo v Kerry players ratings as Ryan O’Donoghue inspires his county to historic victory - Irish Mirror
content: Mayo's Ryan O'Donoghue celebrates after the match (Image: ©INPHO/Ryan Byrne) 1. Jack Livingstone (7) - Faultless for the goal and got to grips with the Kerry press as the game wore on. 2. Jack Coyne (8) - Solid as a rock and didn't give Dylan Geaney a sniff all day. 3. Donnacha McHugh (7) - Left exposed one-on-one with David Clifford for Kerry's first-half goal. Grew into the game and held his own thereafter. 4. Eoin McGreal (7) - Tailed Paudie Clifford throughout, ensuring the Kerryman didn't have a free ride. Tired in the second half as Clifford led Kerry's fightback. 5. Sam Callinan (7) - Did so much of the unglamorous work off the ball that drove Mayo on. 6. David McBrien (8) - Punched holes all day long, driving Mayo forward from deep. 7. Enda Hession (8) - Started many of Mayo's attacks from deep and provided the final ball for several scores. 8. Bob Tuohy (8) - Broke a mountain of ball and was particularly effective at the start of the second half when Mayo hit their purple patch. 9. Jack Carney (8) - Started nervously but grew into the contest. Kicked a wonderful two-pointer when Mayo needed it before adding another in the 44th minute. 10. Diarmuid O'Connor (7) - Diligent with the dirty work but didn't do much of note in possession. 11. Paul Towey (6) - Not his day. Replaced before the 25-minute mark after dropping one effort short. 12. Jordan Flynn (8) - Ran himself into the ground and kicked a superb late score when Mayo needed it. 13. Darragh Beirne (9) - Scored the crucial goal that brought Sam Maguire back to Mayo. Mayo's Darragh Beirne celebrates with the Sam Maguire Cup (Image: ©INPHO/Tom O’Hanlon) 14. Ryan O'Donoghue (9) - A magnificent two-pointer kept Mayo in touch in the first half. Played much deeper than usual and showed immense leadership when the game was in the melting pot. 15. Kobe McDonald (8) - Full of running throughout. Shook off a few early misses to get his score and was always positive in possession while tackling tirelessly. 16. Tommy Conroy (8) (on for Paul Towey, 25 mins) - Lively from the moment he entered the fray and fisted over the insurance point to end 75 years of hurt. 17. Matthew Ruane (7) (on for Bob Tuohy, 54 mins) - Kept things simple and played his part down the stretch. 18. Rory Brickenden (7) (on for Eoin McGreal, 54 mins) - Solid defensively during the closing stages. 19. Conor Loftus (7) (on for Diarmuid O'Connor, 57 mins) - Like Ruane, nailed the basics after coming on. 20. Paddy Durcan (7) (on for Sam Callinan, 64 mins) - Not on long enough to make a significant impact. 1. Shane Murphy (7) - Lost just three kickouts in the first half as Kerry edged the kickout battle. Had little chance with Darragh Beirne's goal. 2. Paul Murphy (6) - Had a tough afternoon trying to contain the lively Darragh Beirne. Fortunate to win a free after overcarrying in the first half and also spent time marking Ryan O'Donoghue. 3. Jason Foley (6) - Came into the final in outstanding form. Started well on O'Donoghue but was beaten a couple of times before finishing on Tommy Conroy. 4. Dylan Casey (7) - The pick of the Kerry defence. Fared well against Kobe McDonald early on and can be pleased with his efforts despite ultimately losing the duel. 5. Graham O'Sullivan (6) - Couldn't be faulted for effort and chipped in with a point but wasn't able to influence the game as much as he would have liked. 6. Mike Breen (7) - The gatekeeper of the Kerry defence. Another solid display from a player who has been immense all season. 7. Gavin White (7) - His link play was excellent in the first half but he struggled after the break as his lack of game time this year became apparent. 8. Mark O'Shea (6) - Started brightly before Jack Carney took control of midfield. Lost his man for two crucial two-pointers. 9. Sean O'Brien (7) - Broke even in his battle with Bob Tuohy. Won his share of possession but offered less going forward than in previous outings. 10. Joe O'Connor (7) - Never quite reached the heights of last season but still forced several turnovers and scored a fine point. 11. Sean O'Shea (7) - Excellent in the first half, setting up David Clifford's goal with a delightful pass and scoring three points himself. Missed a few big chances after the break. 12. Tom O'Sullivan (5) - Kicked two poor wides before eventually finding the target. Replaced at half-time after struggling to get up to the pace of the game. 13. Paudie Clifford (9) - Had Kerry won, he would have been a leading contender for Man of the Match. Scored 0-3 and produced some sublime kick-passing. 14. David Clifford (9) - Did everything in his power to keep Sam Maguire in Kerry. His late missed two-point attempt was costly, but he still finished with 1-6 from play. Kerry's David Clifford celebrates after scoring his side's first goal of the match(Image: ©INPHO/Tom Maher) 15. Dylan Geaney (5) - Picked up what looked like an ankle injury early on and never seemed fully fit. Held scoreless by Jack Coyne before being replaced. 16. Keith Evans (6) (on for Tom O'Sullivan, half-time) - Couldn't help swing the momentum back in Kerry's favour. 17. Tomás Kennedy (5) (on for Dylan Geaney, 50 mins) - Given 20 minutes to make an impact, but the young forward found it difficult on the biggest stage. 18. Brian Ó Beaglaoich (5) (on for Graham O'Sullivan, 58 mins) - His absence from the starting team was keenly felt. Kerry will hope his injury troubles are behind him next season. 19. Evan Looney (6) (on for Mark O'Shea, 64 mins) - Did remarkably well to win possession before Sean O'Shea's late effort. 20. Micheál Burns (5) (on for Joe O'Connor, 67 mins) - Only had a brief cameo and wasn't able to influence the outcome. title: The Toyota Prius Makes The Honda HR-V Look Thirsty And Sluggish, And They Cost The Same - CarBuzz
content: Justin Pritchard is a seasoned Sudbury, Ontario-based automotive journalist, producer, and technical writer. With a passion for cars and a talent for storytelling, he's established himself as a prominent figure in the Canadian automotive scene. His work, which encompasses automotive reviews, insightful analyses, and stunning photography, is featured across multiple Canadian television programs, print publications, and online platforms. Justin's dedication to his craft has earned him numerous awards and accolades, solidifying his reputation as a trusted voice in the automotive industry. Most shoppers today buy SUVs, not cars, as a default solution for practicality and fuel efficiency. Could the Toyota Prius be the ultimate anti-crossover of the SUV scene? This slick, sleek hybrid hatch is a few hundred dollars worth of roof-mounted cargo carrier away from SUV storage capacity, and could cut your gas bill in half (or more) compared to something like a Honda HR-V. If you’ve stuck to your guns and avoided buying an SUV for years, the latest Prius is more worth a look today than ever, thanks to its latest-generation platform. As we'll see below, Toyota's famous hybrid challenges the compact SUV in numerous metrics, and makes many look thirsty, pricey, and sluggish in comparison. Examining this stacked pricing structure highlights how closely packed the entry-level options are compared to models at the top end. The base HR-V LX FWD has the lowest cost of entry on our list, but adding AWD or moving to the Sport FWD quickly closes the gap on the Prius. At just $28,755, the base Prius LE FWD slots directly between the mid-tier HR-V variants. Notice how the base Prius undercuts several mid-tier HR-V trims while including safety tech the HR-V charges extra for. But price parity only matters if the Prius can actually compete on what drivers experience behind the wheel. The Prius range also gives shoppers more high-end options to consider, with the HR-V line capped at $31,950 for a top-tier EX-L AWD, and the Prius range pushing beyond $37,000 for a Limited AWD. From a strategy standpoint, the HR-V sticks to an accessible $5,350 price span across all trims, but the Prius expands its reach across a broader $8,400 range, allowing for shoppers after higher-end tech and premium features. So the Prius matches the HR-V on price and beats it on standard features — but does it actually perform better, or does the hybrid system sacrifice driver engagement for fuel savings? The Prius doesn't just sip less fuel – it's genuinely faster than the HR-V, reaching 60 mph in under 7.5 seconds versus the Honda's nine-plus. Here's why the hybrid system makes that possible. With its hybrid system supplementing the gas engine, drivers get 194 horsepower in front-drive models and 196 hp with AWD. Note that the Prius’ AWD system uses an electric rear "e-axle", electrically driving the rear wheels without the need of a driveshaft for a physical connection to the front section of the powertrain. Numerous other Toyota models use this setup, as well. The HR-V instead uses a traditional AWD system and a traditional four-cylinder engine of 2-liter displacement, no hybrid gear added. That's good for 158 hp, giving the Prius an output advantage of 36 to 38 hp. While Toyota doesn’t provide a net torque output figure for it, the hybrid-electric torque from the Prius engine makes for low-rpm throttle response that’s sharper and more responsive than the HR-V’s, not to mention quieter. Between this pair, the Prius is the racier machine, not only in looks, but also in performance. Both the Prius and HR-V have fairly noisy engines, though the Prius manages some redemption by way of smoother and snappier performance to back it up. Both machines come in front- or all-wheel drive, both run a CVT transmission in all configurations, each runs just fine on 87-octane gas, and neither has a towing rating. According to EPA data, the Honda HR-V gets 28 combined MPG with front-wheel drive and 27 combined MPG with AWD, resulting in an annual fuel cost of $2,200 to $2,300. By comparison, the Toyota Prius delivers an impressive 57 combined MPG with front-wheel drive and 54 combined MPG with AWD, cutting annual fuel expenses down to around $1,125. The gas cost penalty of adding AWD to either machine is negligible, with the HR-V’s AWD system costing an extra $100 in fuel, and the Prius adding just $50 to your annual gas bill. In dollar terms, the Prius will cost about $1,125 per year less on fuel than the HR-V, despite its performance and output advantage. In this comparison, Toyota’s hybrid system gives drivers a 24-percent horsepower boost, while cutting fuel costs in half. If you keep either of these machines for five years, that amounts to nearly $6,000 saved on fuel costs alone. Beyond that, there is an additional penalty that the Prius allows HR-V shoppers to avoid. Driving the Honda HR-V in the city brings fuel efficiency down by as much as six miles per gallon, adding 20 percent to fuel consumption in city-cycle driving versus highway cruising. On the other hand, the Prius gets roughly the same fuel economy whether it's being driven in the city or on the highway, and the hybrid system actually makes front-drive Prius variants slightly more fuel efficient in the city (57 MPG) than on the highway (56 MPG). So, in addition to drinking about half the fuel of a Honda HR-V overall, the Prius' hybrid tech also shrinks the roughly 20-percent city-driving fuel consumption penalty to virtually nothing, or even reverses it slightly. Long-distance drivers should take note of the EPA-provided range figures as well: the Prius can go up to 644 miles with FWD, compared to the HR-V’s 392-mile figure. That’s an extra 252 miles per tank in the Prius, a64 percent advantage in driving distance versus the HR-V.On paper, the Prius dominates – but paper specs don't capture the one area where the HR-V fights back hard. Is a Prius a viable alternative to a slower, thirstier crossover SUV like the Honda HR-V? Maybe. When deciding between these two machines, it is important to bear a few additional factors in mind. Consider overall height. The HR-V sits about 7 to 8 inches taller than the Prius, a factor to consider if you’ll frequently be loading and unloading roof-mounted gear. If you’re on the vertically challenged side, the Prius’ roof-mounted accessories will prove easier to reach. Though the Prius cuts the fuel bill in half, it also has considerably less ground clearance than the HR-V. On the plus side, that helps with a sportier and more car-like ride that some drivers will like. On the downside, less ground clearance limits off-road capability, and can be an issue for drivers in climates that frequently see heavy snow and road slush. The HR-V has a suspension tuned for all-round comfort, and ride quality stands up well on rough road surfaces. Many drivers will find the Prius to feel sportier and more agile, though noisier and harsher when encountering poorly maintained asphalt. The HR-V offers the more spacious cabin overall, with 97.3 to 98.7 cubic feet of total passenger volume compared to the Prius’ 91.2 cu ft. That’s an advantage of at least seven percent for the HR-V, which also wins on headroom in both seating rows by no less than 0.4 inches and as much as 1.6 inches, depending on trim grade and seating position. Look for 1–4 percent more headroom for the HR-V driver, and more than 4 percent (1.6 inches) for rear-seat occupants versus the Prius. The Prius gives front occupants 1.3 inches (3 percent) more legroom, while the HR-V prioritizes rear passengers with significantly more rear legroom than the Prius, beating it by 2.9 inches (over 8 percent). Wide-shouldered occupants will have a better time in the HR-V as well, since it offers 1.3 inches more room up front and 2.4 inches more in the rear. Front hip room is virtually a dead heat, with the Prius holding a slight advantage, but pulling ahead significantly in rear hip room, where it beats the HR-V by 4.3 inches. On cargo hauling capability, the base Prius LE matches the HR-V almost cubic-foot for cubic-foot, offering 23.8 cu ft of space compared to the HR-V’s 24.4 cu ft. That’s a negligible difference of just 0.6 cu ft, roughly the volume of a medium-sized kitchen microwave oven. Stepping up to higher Prius trims (XLE, Nightshade, Limited) drops cargo capacity slightly to 20.3 cu ft due to interior packaging. Toyota doesn’t list a seats-folded cargo metric for the Prius, though we know the HR-V has the practical advantage of its shape when its rear seats are folded down, opening cargo volume up to 55.1 cu ft. Ultimately, the Prius might not be an outright compact SUV killer, but it’s a highly worthy alternative for the driver who doesn’t mind giving up a little roominess in exchange for some sleeker style, or installing that bike rack or cargo box when a little extra space is required. Martinez battled through six innings on the mound, and Taegen Johnson came on in relief to help finish it off. title: EXCLUSIVE: Melissa Gilbert V Daveigh Chase - Outraged Star Slams Late Former Child Star's Parents in Blistering Social Media Post - Yahoo Lifestyle Canada
content: An outraged Melissa Gilbert slammed late former child star Daveigh Chase's "stage parents" in an emotional Instagram post that also remembered Chase as "bubbly, sweet and professional." As RadarOnline.com reported, Chase, who reportedly had been living on L.A.'s notorious Skid Row, died on June 16 at age 35. She had long struggled with drug abuse, allegedly hooked on heroin and fentanyl. Melissa Gilbert said Daveigh Chase appeared driven by 'a push or need to perform' for her parents.JM11 / WENN.com / MEGA Her official cause of death was listed as AIDS, while chronic polysubstance use – the use of more than one drug in a short period of time – was a contributing factor. "I only worked with Daveigh a couple of days but I could see she was bright both in countenance and in mind," Gilbert, 62, wrote about her encounter with the young actress over 20 years ago when they costarred in an unaired TV pilot. Will Luxton scored a superb century to help set Yorkshire up for a convincing Metro Bank One-Day Cup win – by 184 runs on DLS – over Sussex Sharks at Hove which also saw Ben Coad star with a maiden List A five-wicket haul. Luxton’s third first-team century – 117 off 115 balls – and second in this competition underpinned Yorkshire’s commanding 325-7 from 48 overs after some late morning rain delayed the contest very briefly. Luxton shared a fourth-wicket 160 with Sam Whiteman, who played very nicely for 74 off 72 balls. The pair hit seven sixes between them, Luxton with four of them. Coad then wreaked havoc at the start of Sussex’s chase, claiming three wickets in his first two overs as Sussex slipped to 7-3. He added a fourth as they crumbled to 21-5 and failed to recover, being bowled out for 140 inside 28 overs. The hosts were chasing a revised target of 325 in 48 overs and lost by 184 runs on DLS. Coad finished with eye-catching figures of 5-12 from seven overs. Yorkshire have enjoyed a very impressive weekend on the road following Friday’s Group B win over Glamorgan at Neath, and last year’s semi-finalists are looking strong once again. After Yorkshire were inserted, it was a strange old start to the game, with the visitors falling to 24-1 after only eight legitimate balls. Adam Lyth hit three fours as 17 came from the opening over bowled by left-arm seamer Toby Munt before he pulled the first ball of the second for six off another left-arm quick Sean Hunt. The next ball was a wide on a pitch with good pace and carry before Lyth tried to pull the next ball for six and was caught at deep square-leg. Will Bennison was well caught at backward point by Tom Price off Hunt not long afterwards, and when James Wharton was run out without scoring – a direct hit at the striker’s end by Jack Leaning at backward point – Yorkshire were 75-3 in the 11th over. Picture by Eva Gilbert/Sussex Cricket. Will Luxton on the attack en-route to a seaside century today. Luxton and Whiteman united and confidently advanced Yorkshire’s cause on a pitch with decent pace and carry, albeit the latter offered a sharp return chance to young seamer Freddie Hill on 29. Luxton, aged 23, reached his fifty in 50 balls, and left-handed Whiteman later got to his in 60. Luxton hit back-to-back sixes over long-off and long-on against the seam of Ollie Kirtley – son of ex-Sussex and England quick James – added to two fours in the 31st over as he moved to 97 and the score to 192-3. Whiteman had only just reached his fifty by the time Luxton got to his third first-team hundred in 99 balls. Two of Luxton’s centuries have come in this competition – the first against Warwickshire at Rugby in 2024 – and the other in the Championship earlier this season. That four-day ton was also against the Bears at Scarborough. Whiteman hit all three of his sixes over the leg-side as he and Luxton stepped on the gas. Unfortunately, both departing in the space of three overs, leaving the score at 248-5 in the 39th, meant that Yorkshire didn’t get quite as many as looked likely at one stage. But even with 325 on the board, it always felt like being more than enough against an inexperienced Sussex side who had lost their first two matches. Whiteman was brilliantly caught one-handed by Fynn Hudson-Prentice at cover off Munt before Luxton hoisted the same bowler out to long-off. They had shared Yorkshire’s highest fourth-wicket partnership in List A matches against Sussex. Picture by Eva Gilbert/Sussex Cricket. Sam Whiteman impressed for 74. Fin Bean and captain Dom Bess also fell before George Hill and Kuldeep Yadav shared a quick-fire unbroken 42 for the eighth wicket inside the last four overs of the innings. Hill finished 40 not out and Kuldeep 22 unbeaten against a home side who opted not to bowl experienced heads Hudson-Prentice and Tom Price so they could give experience to others. Having missed a little over three months of first-team action from mid-April with a torn side, Coad returned to Yorkshire’s team for this competition’s opener against Hampshire at Scarborough on Tuesday, a game Yorkshire lost. He struck once before not playing at Neath. With Anthony McGrath able to rotate his seamers in this competition, Coad was back in and put the final nails in a Sussex coffin which was pretty much shut at the midway point in this fixture. He had openers Charlie Tear and George Thomas caught behind and bowled, the latter losing his middle stump, added to Tom Price lbw in his first two overs as the score fell to 7-3 in the fourth. Dan Ibrahim was then caught behind before Ben Cliff had ex-Yorkshire batter Jack Leaning caught at mid-wicket by Whiteman with his first ball. That left Sussex at 21-5 in the 11th over, with Cliff striking with his first ball for the second game running having done so on Friday as well. Hudson-Prentice counter-attacked for 50 off 30 balls, including a couple of sixes. But it only added some kind of respectability to things. And even then, Yorkshire’s margin of victory was a landslide one. Picture by Eva Gilbert/Sussex Cricket. Ben Coad excelled with the new ball to help Yorkshire claim their second win in three Group B matches. Lyth struck twice in his first over, including getting Hudson-Prentice caught at long-on the ball after reaching his fifty. When Freddie Price chipped a return catch two balls later, Sussex were 93-7 in the 20th over. Kuldeep bowled a cutting Munt shortly afterwards, uprooting middle and leg stumps before Sussex captain Jack Carson, like Hudson-Prentice had done, also counter-attacked and hit three leg-side sixes off a Kuldeep over which cost 23. title: Burnham v Starmer: one week in, how do their leadership styles compare? | Labour - The Guardian
content: From TikTok appearances to ‘sugar rush’ policies, new prime minister is taking different approach to predecessor Six weeks ago Andy Burnham was not even an MP; now the former mayor of Greater Manchester is the most important political figure in Britain. After orchestrating a bloodless coup against Keir Starmer, in which he was crowned as Labour leader unopposed, the new prime minister has started his tenure in Downing Street with some eye-catching policies and a radically different approach to communication. A week into the job, how do their leadership styles compare? Ever since his first big speech at the People’s History Museum in Manchester, at which he took no questions but made all the headlines anyway, Burnham has resisted media scrutiny. He did just three interviews as an MP before becoming prime minister – and since entering No 10 has had a brief huddle with political editors and several broadcast pool clips. Instead, his early focus seems to be on social media, answering softball questions on Reddit, appearing alongside viral TikTok stars Bus Aunty and Max Klymenko, and replying to X posts by members of the public. While Keir Starmer has upped his social media game in recent weeks, his Downing Street operation recognised that “traditional” media still had power to drive the narrative and – while he didn’t much like it – he regularly subjected himself to scrutiny. Burnham’s team say he will take more questions, but it hasn’t happened yet. Before he became prime minister, Burnham promised to do politics differently, and he didn’t just mean wearing T-shirts and jeans. “I want to answer questions honestly in this job … I’m determined to keep working in that way.” One of his big selling points with Labour MPs was that he could connect more naturally with the public than Starmer, who was often criticised for sticking to the script and coming across as wooden. But, as Burnham has already found, his words now carry greater weight. He has already been accused of performing U-turns over issues including raising the income tax threshold – when he was really just speaking openly about his ideas before they were fully formed. “It’s funny, these days you can’t answer a question honestly without then people reading everything else into it,” he said. His critics may call him naive, but his more relaxed style may go down well with the public. Grabbing public attention has been one of the big ambitions for Burnham’s first week in office – partly so voters know he’s there, but also to show that he’s different from Starmer, and will shout about what his government is doing. As a result, there have been a series of “sugar rush” cost of living announcements designed to give the public some much-needed breathing space – a VAT cut on electricity bills, a £2 bus fare cap and a 20% business rate cut for pubs. In contrast, Starmer wanted to focus on long-term solutions over what he called “short-term sticking plasters”. Burnham’s energy bills announcement – the equivalent of reducing electricity bills by £45 a year on average – crystallised their different approaches. It is to be paid for by scrapping the digital ID system, which advocates argue could have saved the government tens of billions in the long term by making public services more efficient. The question remains: what happens when the sugar hit wears off? Burnham’s first big announcement on returning to Westminster was that he was going to set up No 10 North as the “nerve centre of a rewired Britain” to oversee a devolution of power and resources across the UK. While opposition parties have dismissed this as a gimmick, the new PM says he is determined to oversee a genuine shift of power from Whitehall to local communities via his Manchester operation. Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters Yet he has also created a powerful new PM’s department taking in both No 10s, parts of the Cabinet Office, Treasury and housing ministry – all overseen by his close ally Louise Haigh, to become the “dominant driver of the UK’s economy”. Antonia Romeo, the United Kingdom’s most senior civil servant, has reportedly been given a seat in the coveted space of No 10’s outer office just outside the prime minister’s study. Starmer also promised to kickstart a new era of devolution, passing a bill allowing mayors to ask for new powers at the end of April – just before the local election trouncing that precipitated his downfall. He also pledged to reverse what he called “the tepid bath of managed decline” in Whitehall, putting his chief secretary, Darren Jones, in charge of its “rewiring” in January this year. Jones said civil servants who did not meet expectations would be “shown the door” – in the end, he followed his boss through it six months later. Burnham, who first became an MP in 2001 before resigning to become mayor of Greater Manchester in 2017, is steeped in the party’s lores and traditions. Back in 2009 he told the Guardian that the three most important things in his life, aside from family, were “Everton FC, the Labour party and the Catholic church – in that order”. After becoming a candidate to lead the party at his third time of asking, he insisted in a letter to the parliamentary Labour party that he would never use party discipline to “stifle debate” and wanted to create a “different culture where everyone has a part to play”. MPs, apart from angry Starmer loyalists, lapped it up. Not least because of the contrast to the hard line against dissent that Starmer and his team showed in the early days of his tenure, when many were suspended for defying the party line. But there are already those questioning Burnham’s pledge to end factional infighting after he removed or demoted more than half of the outgoing prime minister’s cabinet in his first reshuffle.

title: The 2023 Honda HR-V's Rear Glass Keeps Exploding, and Honda Still Won't Call It a Recall - Yahoo Autos
content: Honda's 2023 HR-V has racked up 681 complaints in the federal government's public safety database, and going through them one by one reveals a startling pattern: nearly three out of every four describe the exact same part failing the exact same way. Owners describe a loud bang, a spray of pebbled glass across the cargo area, and a rear window that used to exist. No rock, no accident, no slammed tailgate. Just tempered glass calling it quits on its own. I pulled the raw complaint data straight from NHTSA's public complaints database rather than relying on anyone else's tally, and the math is hard to ignore. Of the 681 complaints filed against the 2023 HR-V, 521 explicitly use words like "shattered" or "exploded" to describe what happened to the rear glass. That's roughly 76 percent of everything owners have bothered to report to the government about this specific model year. For comparison, that ratio would be unusual even for a vehicle under a recognized safety recall, where complaints are typically split across a dozen different gripes. Here, the backglass problem doesn't just lead the pack. It basically is the pack. The complaints haven't slowed down with time, either. The most recent one in the database is dated July 11, 2026, three full years after the redesigned HR-V went on sale. Later model years show a dramatically smaller share of shattering reports: the 2024 HR-V has logged 107 total complaints with only 6 mentioning shattered glass, and 2025 and 2026 models show similarly low ratios. That points to Honda changing something on the assembly line, but whatever changed didn't retroactively fix the first-year trucklets already on the road. Tempered glass is designed to do exactly what these owners are describing when it fails: it doesn't crack, it disintegrates almost instantly into a pile of small, rounded pebbles, because that's the entire point of tempering glass for occupant safety in a crash. The problem isn't that the glass shatters. That's the feature working as intended. The problem is what's triggering it to shatter with nobody around to cause an impact. Owners overwhelmingly report failures near the rear defroster, in cold weather, or shortly after using the defroster switch, which points toward a thermal stress issue at the spot where the glass bonds to the body. Honda's own paperwork backs that theory up. In a technical service bulletin filed with NHTSA, American Honda tells its dealers plainly what happened: during assembly, the urethane sealer used to bond the rear glass to the body made contact with the embedded defroster heating element on some vehicles. That contact point creates a localized hot spot, and repeated heating and cooling there is enough to fracture tempered glass that would otherwise sit there for years without issue. It isn't a rock. It isn't damage you can spot on a pre-purchase inspection. It's a manufacturing tolerance problem baked into the glass before the car ever left the factory. Here's the part that should actually bother HR-V owners: this never became a recall. NHTSA's own recall database lists exactly three safety recalls tied to the 2023 HR-V, covering a seat belt pretensioner missing a rivet, a fuel pump campaign shared across several Honda models, and a steering-related campaign. None of them touch the rear glass. Instead, Honda handled the shattering problem through a July 2024 dealer bulletin it labeled a voluntary product update, a category of repair campaign that sits entirely outside the legal machinery of the National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act. There was no public press release, no NHTSA-tracked completion rate, and no mailer that shows up when a future buyer runs a VIN through a standard recall check. It's the same regulatory gray area other automakers lean on when a problem doesn't clearly cross the line into an unreasonable safety risk. Land Rover recently used a stop-sale rather than a recall to freeze deliveries of the Defender, Discovery, and Range Rover over an unresolved airbag question, and NHTSA typically only forces the issue after the fact, the way it's currently doing with its investigation into the Tesla that plowed into a Texas home. Manufacturers get real latitude to make the first call on whether a defect is safety-related, and that latitude is exactly what keeps a problem like this one out of the recall system. That distinction is not just semantics. A federally logged safety recall has to be free for the life of the vehicle regardless of who owns it, comes with mandatory owner notification timelines, and gets tracked by NHTSA until the repair rate is reported. A product update is a goodwill gesture Honda gets to define, limit to a specific VIN range, and close out on its own schedule. If you're shopping for a used 2023 HR-V, the standard NHTSA VIN lookup that most buyers rely on to check for open recalls will come back clean on this issue even if the rear glass has never been inspected. The move is to call Honda's campaign center directly at 1-888-234-2138 and have the dealer check the VIN against the July 2024 product update, because it won't turn up anywhere else. If your rear glass lets go while you're driving, don't assume you're stuck paying for it out of pocket. Comprehensive coverage, not collision, is what typically pays out for a shattered window with no impact involved, and some states waive the deductible entirely for glass claims. Coverage details vary enough by insurer and state that it's worth an actual conversation with your agent rather than a guess, especially if you're weighing whether a higher-deductible policy still makes sense for a car with a known glass problem. Whatever allowed sealant to migrate onto a live heating element for an entire model year, the bigger takeaway is how little visibility car buyers actually have into problems automakers choose to handle quietly. The HR-V's rear glass isn't an isolated fluke. It's a clear look at how much daylight exists between a recall and everything else automakers call instead, and why that gap is worth understanding before you're the one standing in a parking lot staring at a hole where your back window used to be. title: V Girls: Julia Cumming on Stepping Into the Solo Spotlight - V Magazine
content: The musician discovering herself through the most personal creative process of her career The musician discovering herself through the most personal creative process of her career With nothing to hide and everything to say, Julia Cumming is claiming center stage on her own terms—living, performing, and creating exactly as she declares in her hit single “My Life”: “My life is mine.” Making space to love hard, learn, and grow, all while making her name as a solo act, Cumming found her footing through Sunflower Bean, the band where she first made her name in music. Now, the artist has rediscovered her voice while creating her eponymous solo album. “I get to learn and create myself again as a performer! It’s both very familiar and entirely new,” she explains. The moment she decided to go solo, she says “was as soon as I wrote ‘My Life.’ I knew immediately that there was a new voice coming through, one that I needed to develop and discover.” The experience has been liberating, but one that Cumming approaches with gratitude. “Having the freedom to explore topics and ideas without wondering if they are speaking for a whole group” is the gift her solo album has given her, she explains. The entire process was lengthy, taking a total of three years from first imagining to finally completing the album. Her in-depth creative process is one that doesn’t shy away from discomfort. “I had to spend a lot of time in some tough places in my mind,” she explains. This internal contemplation informs her writing, a process that shows in her music. “I really had to look hard into my subconscious and find out what was going on in there. That could be a painful and strange process. Sometimes feelings came out that were surprising or scary, or heartbreaking,” she says. With inspirations for the album stemming from Joni Mitchell, Carole King, and Judee Sill, all with the aesthetics of LA’s Laurel Canyon in the 1970s, Cumming sought to create an active listening experience rather than a passive one, transporting the listener and asking them to recognize themselves within her vision. But music isn’t the only act in Cumming’s new one-woman show. She’s made a name for herself in fashion, modeling for brands like Anna Sui, Diesel, and Schiaparelli, as well as film, making acting debut in director Edgar Wright’s 2025 film The Running Man. title: Sharon V. Frankenfield (Violette) - Star Tribune
content: Fridley - Age 89 of Fridley, passed away on July 9, 2026, at Regions Hospital after a brief illness with her loving family by her side. Sharon was born on June 24, 1937, and raised in Northeast Minneapolis and attended St. Anthony of Padua School Catholic High School. On January 27, 1957, she married Raymond Frankenfield and together they raised five rambunctious sons. They later divorced. Sharon was a Licensed Practical Nurse and, later in life, returned to Anoka-Ramsey CC where she obtained her Registered Nurse degree. She worked as a labor and delivery nurse at St. Andrew's Hospital, St. Barnabas Hospital, Metropolitan Medical Center, and finally at Hennepin County Medical Center. Her colleagues were an integral part of her life, and many of them became lifelong friends. The bravest among them allowed her to join their golf group which continues today. Sharon was independent, strong-willed, compassionate, and the loving center of her family; she was rarely at a loss for words—often giving encouragement or advice. Raising five boys was one of her greatest achievements, and she made every effort to be there for each one of them or their families whenever they needed her. Pictures of her family adorned her walls in all her residences throughout her life, and she paid tribute to the past and the present with numerous photos of her family and friends. Her sons often teased her about her culinary skills, but she loved to entertain, to show off her latest concoctions, and was always up for lunch or dinner at one of her favorite restaurants. The goodbye hugs were deep, heartfelt, and always followed by "I love you." Sharon's lifelong hobby was knitting, and her numerous mittens, hats, sweaters, shawls, blankets and kitchen rags can be found all over the United States. She could talk and knit at the same speed without even looking at her knitting needles. After her retirement, Sharon traveled extensively in the United States but also throughout Europe and the Pacific. Sharon's final residence for the past three years was at Hayden Grove Senior Living in St. Anthony where she was surrounded by many former residents of Northeast Minneapolis who shared her passions for cards, board games, emojis, and family. She was preceded in death by her parents George and Fern Violette; infant grandson Ross Allen Frankenfield; and brother-in-law Timothy Ready. Sharon is survived by sons Michael (Kelly), John (Beth), Greg (Marissa), Tom (Bonni) and Dave (Laura) Frankenfield; many grandchildren and great-grandchildren; brother George Jr. (Mary Kay) Violette; sisters Linda (Mike Sr.) Ojile; Mary Jo (Bruce) Durand; her ex-husband Raymond (Bev) Frankenfield; and a host of nieces, nephews, loving relatives and friends. A Celebration of Life service for Sharon will be held on August 29, 2026, at the Old Log Theater beginning with a visitation at 11:00 AM and a brief service offered by Father Henry Doyle at 12:30 PM. Food and fellowship will follow until 3:00 PM. Sharon's final wishes were that gifts or donations could be made in her name to Camp Knutson (campknutson.lssmn.org).    www.billmanhunt.com To send flowers to the family or plant a tree in memory of Sharon, please visit our floral store. title: Kerry v Mayo: No drama and defending champions will collect a 40th All-Ireland title - The Irish Times
content:
Are All-Ireland finals ever this straightforward? The almost regretful consensus that Kerry will inevitably win this weekend’s final surely can’t simply materialise as uncomplicatedly as bookmakers’ odds and punditry are forecasting? Unfortunately, from a Mayo perspective, it happens quite often. Kerry are favourites for good reason. Defending champions, they convincingly won last year by ramping up performance levels in Croke Park and delivering a season’s best display in the final. Now, the same management in charge of much the same players is back on the big day. But rather than facing an existential challenge, such as many believed Donegal posed 12 months ago, Kerry are confronted by unexpected opponents who scarcely featured on the radar as recently as a month ago. The All-Ireland hurling final a week ago provides indications of what can happen when an experienced team with medals in their pockets take on rising newcomers. Limerick’s crushing win over Galway can be spun either way: the inevitable outcome of that scenario or a further cushioning of Mayo as outsiders. If that implies Kerry are vulnerable to the assumptions of complacency – fair enough – but it is more likely that, for Jack O’Connor and his crew, the hurling final just hardened the belief that if they work as hard as they should in the biggest match of the year, they are likely winners given their other advantages. The exaggerated jumpiness of the champions in the face of perceived “disrespect”, as evidenced by O’Connor intervening in the “bridesmaid” advertisement controversy, tells its own tale. Mayo’s semi-final against Louth may have been bloodless, but they had been well tempered in other All-Ireland matches against Monaghan, Tyrone, Meath and Cork. Tight matches are tight matches regardless, and the lessons learned are valuable. Balancing that, the only other Division One team Mayo played – given Monaghan’s relegation and Meath and Cork having played in the second tier this season – was Tyrone, who beat them. That match in Omagh is significant because Mayo were only narrowly edged out and it’s one formline through Kerry that gives reason for optimism. Tyrone ran the champions as close as possible without quite looking like they would actually win, but they also lost out to a couple of controversial refereeing decisions. There are other lines of optimism. Kerry’s full back line has not looked waterproof, whereas Mayo’s full forwards were rampant against Louth, the sharp, youthful corners, Darragh Beirne and the phenomenon that is Kobe McDonald, were individually irrepressible and shepherded most effectively by the in-form Ryan O’Donoghue. Since the dismal beating by Roscommon, Mayo have been on a consistently upwards trajectory. Can they accelerate or at least maintain that? John O’Keeffe, the distinguished former Kerry player and coach, was a football analyst with The Irish Times for many years. In advance of the 2013 All-Ireland final, in Jim Gavin’s first year, he urged caution as Dublin’s exuberant young guns - Jack McCaffrey, Paul Mannion and Ciarán Kilkenny - faced into their first senior final either still in or just out of their teens. He had played his first final in 1970 as a teenager and, frankly, said it had passed him by, the frenetic movement and tension of the occasion making him focus on survival more than anything more impactful. All three of the young Dublin players had been replaced with 30 minutes to go, and only Mannion, in early exchanges, was injured. Yet, all three went on to have extraordinary senior careers. All that can be said with certainty about Sunday is that it will be a big challenge for Beirne and McDonald to replicate their semi-final form in the pressure cooker intensity of the All-Ireland final. On a more practical level, how well supplied will they be? All year, Mayo have lacked a traditional centrefield presence, something that’s even more important in these days of the new rules. They can argue that Louth’s very strong middle third also edged the battle of the restarts but lost by 17 points. For all the resolve to dominate the breaks, that’s not easy when Kerry have the O’Connors at wing forward, as well as Paudie Clifford roaming around the breakdown and also the pace of Gavin White tearing through. All of which is to leave the biggest question marks until last. David Clifford comes into the final yet again as the football of the year front-runner. In that form, he has rarely disappointed on big days. His management of the final kick-out in the Tyrone quarter-final was exemplary, reading the break, directing the play and providing the assist for the goal that put a flattering veneer on the scoreline. His menace is so constant as to be almost unremarkable, as well as unmarkable. He has added a rallying element to his performances, working the crowd and getting them involved as he lays waste opponents. David Byrne did a good job on him for Dublin in the semi-final but, as ever, it was a co-operative effort as it will be for Mayo. Byrne is a vastly experienced defender with eight All-Ireland medals. Clifford still shot 0-5 from play to go with his goal from a penalty rebound. Seán O’Shea is fully restored after injury and he too poses a serious scoring threat, whereas Dylan Geaney, relatively quiet against Dublin, still took until his 19th attempt of the championship in an All-Ireland semi-final before he missed a first shot at goal, having racked up 0-22. It’s not that they’re unopposed and Jack Coyne, if not quite at last year’s levels, is an accomplished corner back, whereas Eoin McGreal brings pace. At full back, Donnchadh McHugh is expected to be handed the Clifford brief, with another speedy defender Enda Hession a possible match for the brother. Sam Callinan and the excellent David McBrien will make sure the middle third is well contested. These are all best-case scenarios for Mayo to be as competitive as possible because, if they are not going to win, the future of the team demands a respectable contest with the potential to return as contenders. Kerry, though, have a single-item agenda: be the first county to win a 40th senior All-Ireland. Expect that box to be ticked. title: V.com weekend vote: How much do you feel you can afford to pay for a set of strings? - Violinist.com
content: We have thousands of human-written stories, discussions, interviews and reviews from today through the past 20+ years. Find them here: July 25, 2026, 7:20 PM · This week the German-based string company Pirastro announced the release of a string set aimed at affordability, selecting some of its most popular strings for set that maximizes quality while offering a reasonable price point. Global inflation certainly has hit the world of violin, viola, cello and bass strings, affecting the prices of premium string lines in all brands, particularly in strings that contain precious metals such as silver and gold. (And in fact, some super-premium violin strings have spiked as high as nearly $500.) How does one cope? Many of us will simply shell out more to get the string brands we know, like and trust. Or we might change the strings a little less often. Or, we might look for quality at a lower price point. How are you feeling these days about the prices of violin strings, and particularly, what do you feel willing to pay for a set? Please participate in the vote below (which is in U.S. dollars, here is a converter if you need to figure this out for Euros, Canadian $, etc.). Then let us know your thoughts about the price of strings and how you are coping. July 26, 2026 at 12:45 AM · I've been fortunate in that the price of my current preferred viola strings (D'Addario Kaplan Amo) hasn't really changed since 2021. There have been a few temporary price increases due to supply chain interruptions, but the price has always dropped back down within two or three months. That said, inflation has made me more reluctant to try other strings. I've been meaning to try Peter Infeld, and I likely would have done it earlier this year if the price was still where it was 4-5 years ago. July 26, 2026 at 01:03 AM · As a pensioner, I tend to work out what things cost per month, and strings are a small part of my outgoings, so really the top price is more of a gut feeling. Luckily the Vision family suits my violin the best, so my upper limit is more or less fixed for me. I wonder if per month viola and cello strings cost the same as violin strings. July 26, 2026 at 05:16 AM · Many string sets now exceed $150 retail. July 26, 2026 at 11:57 AM · I don't change my strings but annually at most, so it's okay if they're more expensive.  I did find I like Warchal strings on my viola and my luthier can get them for $125. July 26, 2026 at 01:52 PM · I can get Visions for my viola for $100, so that works for me. July 26, 2026 at 02:51 PM · It's definitely gotten out of hand. If the higher-end strings lasted much longer than, say, Dominants, that'd be one thing, but I've found that pretty much any string set has noticeably declined after around 120 hrs of play, and at that point I'd rather just be playing a fresh set of Dominants I can get on sale for $58 rather than feeling guilty about having to stretch the lifespan of $140 Rondos to get my money's worth. July 26, 2026 at 03:36 PM · Yeah, I got Visions on my viola, Tom. But it's only a $500 viola, so there's no need to experiment further. It would be like putting lipstick on a pig. Lol. July 26, 2026 at 04:10 PM · My price limit would be whatever Pirastro gut Gold label is.  Finding the optimum set of strings is the least expensive way to improve the sound and response of a violin, but-- putting expensive strings on my inexpensive violins would be money half-wasted. July 26, 2026 at 04:33 PM · As a string program administrator, the cost of strings really adds up in our annual maintenance budget. Most of our teachers hate preludes so I had been working on finding a budget set that would be acceptable. Tonicas were already the right set. They sound similar enough to Dominants that teachers are happy and as the mom of a student in the program, I'm happy too. I tried Ascente and they were not acceptable to my ear. Someone in another comment asked if cello and violas strings have similar annual costs. For our program, yes, because they are hardier and last longer, the annual math works out pretty similarly. July 26, 2026 at 07:03 PM · I missed a sale last week on a new set of strings, and it cost me $30 minus whatever they charge for shipping. I wasn’t happy. But I’m still happy that I can get Thomastik Dominant for less than $100. Does anyone know if the wrapped E sounds better the steel E? Will it hold up? July 26, 2026 at 08:00 PM · Nickie, I can't say whether the wrapped E sounds better or worse, because that will depend on what sound and playing properties you like and dislike. July 26, 2026 at 08:11 PM · I really like the John Pearse® #3510 'ARTISTE'? VIOLIN MEZZO Strings costing around $40. Stephen T Cundall, luthier and owner of Luthier Violin Shop in Commerce Texas, recommended them following a number repairs and adjustments to my 1830's Charotte Millot violin. He assured me that they are very high quality and comparable to much more expensive strings. I like these violin strings so much that I just ordered another violin set and John Pearse strings for my violin, mandolin and guitar to try you out. You can buy them directly at https://breezyridge.biz/  My order of $75 included free shipping. I was impressed by the number of sets and string gauges they offer for various string instruments. My research shows that the John Pierce is a brand is owned by Breezy Ridge, which produces the strings in a dedicated facility near Harrisburg, Pennsylvania. In the recent past I have tried evah pirazzi green, Dominants, Pirastro Tonica, Warchal Karneol, and Tomastik Spirit, Obligato, and Vision strings on my violin. July 26, 2026 at 09:15 PM · @Daniel - my luthier's rule of thumb is to change strings after 120 hours, so I follow that pretty closely.  It has worked well for me. @Gordon - My viola is small (15.5) and a great deal more expensive than yours.  Visions make it sound wonderful.  A professional violist told me "I love the sound of your viola.  So, I will stick with them. July 26, 2026 at 09:51 PM · On my main violin I use Olivs, but I don't do a "set", I pick my own gauges for G,D, and A. And for my E string, I use Evah greens. My cost on my violin with Oliv strings + Evah green E,  is approx. $190 every 3 months. My kids use Evah Green sets on their violins. And it costs me approx. $200 every 3 months or so for both their violins. So my total outlay every 3 months for our main violins is approx. $390 every 3 months. I use Tonicas on my other violins. IMHO, they are very decent strings, plus they're relatively cheap. I'm excited to try the "new" Tonica combo on one of my violins that currently has the regular Tonicas on them. July 26, 2026 at 11:25 PM · I voted $150 to $200, but I'm thinking in Australian dollars which don't buy as much as US dollars. July 26, 2026 at 11:42 PM · I can manage $100-150 USD. I have three fiddles, each with a different setup. I stagger the orders so that I don't have more than one instrument at a time with strings needing a break-in period. Most recent combos I ordered: 1) Warchal Amber - E-A-D-G. These are for my main instrument. 2) Pirastro Obligato - A-D-G + Lenzner/Optima Goldbrokat E. July 27, 2026 at 01:08 AM · I’m happy to get a new set of Tonicas for my 80 year old aunts violin.  She plays for her church and the violin I got her was a built on back German violin from the early 20th century.  I got geared pegs installed and, with a coda bow it is just what she needs.  Many people are probably in her position.   Sometimes pretty good is good enough. You must be registered and logged in to submit a comment. Dimitri Musafia, Master Maker of Violin and Viola Cases

title: Minister Anand meets with His Highness Prince Rahim Aga Khan V - canada.ca
content: The Honourable Anita Anand, Minister of Foreign Affairs, met with His Highness Prince Rahim Aga Khan V in Vancouver today to discuss shared priorities related to international development, economic partnerships, affordable housing and regional security. July 25, 2026 - Vancouver, British Columbia - Global Affairs Canada The Honourable Anita Anand, Minister of Foreign Affairs, met with His Highness Prince Rahim Aga Khan V in Vancouver today to discuss shared priorities related to international development, economic partnerships, affordable housing and regional security. Minister Anand welcomed the progress of the implementation of the Joint declaration between Prime Minister Mark Carney and His Highness the Aga Khan of March 2026 and noted the importance of maintaining momentum on its implementation. The Minister also highlighted the success of the Generations multi-generational housing initiative across Canada, led by the Ismaili Council for Canada, and underscored that affordable housing remains a priority for the Government of Canada. Minister Anand and the Aga Khan discussed the housing partnership announced under the Joint Declaration, a clear example of practical cooperation between Canada and the Ismaili Imamat and welcomed the Memorandum of Understanding between Build Canada Homes and the Ismaili Council for Canada, dedicated to  focused on advancing affordable multi-generational housing and community infrastructure projects across Canada. The Minister also highlighted the continued cooperation through the FinDev Canada-Aga Khan Fund for Economic Development Memorandum of Understanding, which outlines a shared commitment to cooperate and explore potential investment opportunities in infrastructure, renewable energy, agriculture and financial services. The Minister also recognized the Aga Khan Development Network's (AKDN) long-standing presence and expertise in regions facing complex challenges, including Syria, and highlighted its important development partnerships in Pakistan and East Africa, expressing appreciation for its work improving the quality of life through initiatives that address social and economic challenges facing local communities. Minister Anand concluded by recognizing the long-standing contributions of the Ismaili community in Canada through volunteerism, civic engagement, philanthropy and investment in communities across the country, and reaffirmed Canada's commitment to deepening its partnership with the Ismaili Imamat and the AKDN, including through continued collaboration to advance stability, resilience and sustainable development. The Merced County Association of Governments has released the 2026 edition of On the MoVe, its annual community report detailing how Measure V transportation sales tax dollars were spent across Merced County. The voter‑approved half‑cent sales tax generated $26.7 million in revenue during Fiscal Year 2024‑25 and invested nearly $15 million in transportation improvements countywide. The audited financial statements included in the report show, “total revenue: $26,762,905… total expenditure: $14,984,261.” Since Measure V took effect in 2017, the program has produced more than $200 million for road repairs, mobility upgrades and public transit. This year’s report highlights dozens of projects completed between July 2024 and June 2025, ranging from street rehabilitation and bridge replacements to sidewalk infill, bicycle infrastructure and intersection improvements. Every incorporated city in Merced County received Measure V funding, along with county‑maintained roads and regional corridors. Countywide, Measure V supported a wide range of transportation improvements. Examples highlighted in the report include the Lorraine Street Bridge replacement in Dos Palos, Palm Avenue rehabilitation in Merced County, and multiple sidewalk and street repairs in Merced, Livingston and Los Banos. The report also shows $2.3 million spent on alternative transportation modes, including bicycle and pedestrian improvements and investments in zero‑emission transit vehicles. Public transportation continues to play a major role in countywide mobility. Measure V’s free‑fare program provided 202,019 rides on The Bus’ fixed‑route system last fiscal year. Of those trips, 133,358 were taken by seniors, 63,366 by ADA‑eligible passengers and 5,295 by veterans. The report states that the program “helped residents access employment, medical care, shopping and other essential services.” MCAG Executive Director Stacie Guzman said the annual report demonstrates the value of the voter‑approved measure. “Every Measure V dollar spent represents an investment that Merced County residents made in their own communities,” Guzman said. The full 2026 On the MoVe report is available at mcagov.org/onthemove, with free printed copies in English and Spanish at all Merced County city halls and the county administration building.

title: NASA's Saturn V produced 7.6 million pounds of thrust, stood 363 feet tall, and sent 24 astronauts to the Moon without losing one — then in 1973 it was retired, its tooling scrapped, and nothing as powerful left Earth for almost 50 years. - 19FortyFive
content:
From three miles away, the first thing to reach the press site was light. Then the sound arrived as force, shaking tripods and cracking in reporters’ chests. The Saturn V stood 363 feet tall, weighed 6.2 million pounds fully fueled, and made 7.6 million pounds of thrust from five F-1 engines to send 24 astronauts toward the Moon. The legends get the rest wrong: it was one of the loudest machines ever built, near 203 decibels, but it never melted concrete or set grass on fire a mile away. It launched 13 times, never lost a crew, and flew its last in 1973 — after which nothing as powerful left Earth for nearly 50 years. At the press site for an Apollo launch, the reporters and their cameras stood more than three miles from the pad, and even that distance was a compromise between a clear view and plain safety. The Saturn V waited on the horizon, thirty-six stories tall and sheathed in frost from the supercold propellant inside, venting streamers of vapor into the Florida morning. It had reached the pad at walking pace, carried on a tracked crawler the size of a baseball infield that crept along at about a mile an hour, the last quiet thing about the launch. Then the engines lit. The first thing to reach the press site was light, a sudden false sunrise, because light outruns sound. A few seconds later the sound itself arrived, and it came less as noise than as force. Reporters described the ground seeming to come loose underfoot, a pressure that crackled in the chest, tripods and trouser legs shaking three miles from the flame. The rocket rose slowly at first, held down for an instant and then climbing, and only its sheer size disguised how fast it was already moving. What people remembered long afterward was not how it looked but how it felt, the sensation of being struck by a sound. Saturn 5 Rocket. Image from NASA Kennedy Space Center Taken on 6/28/2026. Taken by Harry J. Kazianis for 19FortyFive.com I get that, to a certain extent. A few weeks back, my wife and I went to the Kennedy Space Center here in Florida and spent a few hours staring at the Saturn V rocket on display. All photos in this article are from that visit. One thing you have to get about this rocket: she is massive. The thing making that sound was the largest and most powerful flying machine of its era. The Saturn V stood 363 feet tall, about sixty feet taller than the Statue of Liberty, and fully fueled it weighed roughly 6.2 million pounds. Almost all of that weight was not machine but fuel: the rocket was essentially a thin shell around enormous tanks, drained at a staggering rate of some thirteen tonnes of propellant every second from the first stage alone. It flew in three stages, each burning in turn and then falling away to lighten the load. The first stage carried five engines called the F-1, burning kerosene and liquid oxygen, and together they produced 7.6 million pounds of thrust at liftoff. The F-1 remains the most powerful single-chamber liquid-fueled rocket engine ever flown, and five of them clustered together gave the rocket its power. The upper stages switched to liquid hydrogen, five smaller engines on the second stage and a single restartable engine on the third to push the spacecraft out of Earth orbit and toward the Moon. Everything about it was staged, deliberate, and enormous, and it was built to do one thing that had never been done. Because the launch was so overwhelming to witness, the stories around it grew in the retelling. For decades it was repeated that the Saturn V was so loud it melted the concrete of the launch pad, that it set grass on fire more than a mile away, that its sound was second only to a nuclear detonation. Those claims are largely folklore, and the real story is the more interesting one. Saturn 5 Rocket. Image from NASA Kennedy Space Center, taken on 6/28/2026. Taken by Harry J. Kazianis for 19FortyFive.com In 2022, physicists at Brigham Young University built a physics-based model of a Saturn V launch and published it in the Journal of the Acoustical Society of America. They estimated the sound at about 203 decibels, closely matching a level NASA had recorded from a first-stage test decades earlier. Decibels are logarithmic, so the number is hard to feel: 170 decibels is roughly ten jet engines, and 200 is on the order of ten thousand. It is one of the loudest sounds a machine has ever made. It was not, however, loud enough to melt concrete or start fires. As the study’s lead author, Kent Gee, put it, “Mankind has not produced a sound source” capable of that. Where grass burned near the pad, it burned from radiant heat or falling debris, not from noise. Historical accounts had put the level anywhere from 180 to 235 decibels, a spread that shows how much was eyewitness impression rather than measurement. The true figure needs no embellishment. Two hundred decibels is astonishing on its own. The Saturn V existed because of a sentence. In 1961, President Kennedy committed the United States to landing a man on the Moon and returning him safely before the decade was out, and at the time no one had the machine to do it. American astronauts were still flying brief missions in low Earth orbit. The gap between that and a crewed lunar landing was not a question of willingness but of physics, and the physics demanded a rocket that did not yet exist. Building it became one of the largest peacetime industrial undertakings in American history. The design was led by Wernher von Braun’s team at NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center, and the work spread across the country to hundreds of thousands of workers at thousands of companies and universities, with the three stages built by Boeing, North American Aviation, and Douglas, and the engines by Rocketdyne. In roughly seven years the effort went from the cramped orbital flights of the Gemini program to a vehicle that could lift about 130 tons into orbit and send astronauts to another world. The rocket was the piece that turned a political promise into something that could leave the ground, on schedule. It worked, and it kept working. The Saturn V launched thirteen times between 1967 and 1973 and never once failed to deliver its payload, never lost a crew, and carried twenty-four astronauts to the Moon, beginning with Apollo 11 in 1969. It was not flawless in the way the legend suggests. An early uncrewed test, Apollo 6, was shaken by violent pogo vibration and lost engines mid-ascent, and on Apollo 13 the second stage’s center engine shut down about two minutes early, with the rocket’s own guidance computer firing the remaining engines longer to compensate. The program’s one crew tragedy, the Apollo 1 fire that killed three astronauts in 1967, happened on the ground during a test, atop a smaller rocket, not aboard a Saturn V. Its flight record held to the end. Saturn 5 Rocket. Image from NASA Kennedy Space Center Taken on 6/28/2026. Taken by Harry J. Kazianis for 19FortyFive.com Saturn 5 Rocket. Image from NASA Kennedy Space Center Taken on 6/28/2026. Taken by Harry J. Kazianis for 19FortyFive.com Then, in 1973, after lofting the Skylab space station, the Saturn V flew for the last time. NASA retired it, the specialized tooling was scrapped, and much of the hard-won knowledge scattered into retirements and archives. For nearly fifty years, nothing as powerful left the Earth. Not until 2022 did a rocket of comparable power fly again, and only in April 2026 did a crew fly around the Moon once more, aboard a rocket that at last exceeds the Saturn V’s thrust. The machine that made the Moon reachable had become, for half a century, a capability the country had to build back almost from scratch. Reaching the Moon was the historic achievement. Holding onto the ability to do it, the next fifty years showed, was the harder one. Harry J.
