title: All-Ireland football final: Kerry v Mayo - triumph, pain and 'the curse' - BBC
content: Kerry were victors when they last met Mayo in an All-Ireland final back in 2006 In the build-up to last year's All-Ireland final, former Kerry captain Dara Ó Cinnéide pointed out "nobody has lost more finals than Kerry". It's true, as while the Kingdom lead the way on the roll of honour with 39 Sam Maguire triumphs, their 24 defeats on Gaelic football's biggest day is greater than any other county. Cork are next in that unwanted bracket with 16, but just one behind - level with Galway - sits Mayo. The Yew County must go back 75 years for the last of their three All-Ireland titles, defending the crown they had won the previous season, but while All-Ireland success has eluded them since, a return to the final was 44 years in the making. In 1989, led by the late John O'Mahony, Mayo rolled into Croke Park to face a Cork side that had fallen short in the previous two finals against Meath - the second of those after a replay. Perhaps there was a sense that it was the Rebels' time, but Mayo had their chances, only to fall to a three-point defeat. It would prove to be the first of 11 disappointments on final day. Watch live on BBC Two, BBC Sport website & app from 15:00 They were back seven years later, thanks to a semi-final win over Kerry who were ready to challenge again after a number of years in the wilderness, but after Colm Coyle's late punt hopped off the ground and over the bar to force a draw, Meath won a replay that was marred by an early brawl. Certainly, there was an element of fortune in Meath's equaliser in the drawn game, but could it be something a lot deeper for Mayo? A curse, perhaps? As the story - or myth - goes, following their 1951 win and on their way home on to Castlebar on an open-back lorry, the team's boisterous celebrations interrupted a funeral taking place in Foxford, just outside Ballina with the presiding priest laying a curse that Mayo would not win an All-Ireland title any member of the team was alive. Whether that is fact or folklore remains unclear, but Mayo's fortunes on All-Ireland final day have not improved since. The following year, they returned to the decider against Kerry who would make up for the previous year's semi-final reverse with a three-point win. It would not be misfortune for Mayo, but the brilliance of Maurice Fitzgerald that was the difference, with the Cahersiveen man kicking nine points on the day. Those two meetings between the counties would prove to be the beginning of a new-found rivalry. Kerry won the first of two All-Ireland finals in three years against Mayo in 2004 Kerry would return to the top in 2000, marking the start of a successful decade as Sam Maguire would return to the Kingdom on five occasions, with three further final defeats in this time. In 2004, Mayo were back in the final to meet them and while Alan Dillon netted an early goal, the game would quickly get away from them as Colm Cooper goaled at the other end on a day in which he and Ó Cinnéide starred in an emphatic win as Jack O'Connor led Kerry to his first title as manager. Two years later, Mayo stunned Dublin the last four with Ciaran McDonald landing a sublime winner, but it was the same old story in the final as an early goal blitz paved the way for another handsome win for Kerry. While O'Connor stood down at the end of 2006, Pat O'Shea would guide them to another title title the following season - the last time Kerry achieved back to back All-Irelands, only for Tyrone to deny them three-in-a-row the following year - a repeat of the 2005 decider. Mayo were winners in the 2017 semi-final after a replay As that great Kerry team's powers began to fade by the end of the decade, Mayo would find a new nemesis as after defeat by Donegal in 2012, Dublin would account for them in the 2013 decider, again in 2016 after a replay that was largely down to two first-half own goals in the drawn game, while Dean Rock would break their hearts with a winning free at the death in the 2017 final. However, Kerry and Mayo would serve up some incredible semi-final drama in the 2010s as after Kieran O'Leary salvaged a draw for Kerry at Croke Park, the Kingdom would win after extra-time in a thriller at Limerick's Gaelic Grounds. Three years later at the same stage, it was roles reversed as Paddy Durcan rescued a draw for Mayo who finished the job in the replay thanks to goals from current manager Andy Moran and Diarmuid O'Connor. While the counties lost two All-Ireland finals apiece since that game, Kerry have added two more titles in the third coming of O'Connor. They sides swapped wins in 2022 and 2023, Kerry now an established force led by the talents of the Cliffords, the Geaneys, Gavin White and Sean O'Shea. Mayo contain many survivors of their most recent final defeat by Tyrone in 2021, but a fresh crop have also emerged in Kobe McDonald, Darragh Beirne, Eoin McGreal and Cian McHale. Will the ghosts of All-Ireland finals past continue to haunt Mayo and Kerry cement their place at the top, or will the 75 years of hurt finally come to an end against a county that has handed them three of those 11 defeats since 1951? Sunday will be a day to remember for one set of supporters, while the other will revisit that sense of devastation both know only too well on All-Ireland final day. As for the 'curse'? Well, the last member of the Mayo 1951 panel, Dr Mick Loftus, passed away in 2023. title: Socialists v. the Senate - The Mining Journal -
content: Political parties tend to harshly reject the idea that they are a threat to the constitutional order, but the Democratic Socialists of America are making it part of their brand. The DSA has released a new program that, besides contemplating the advent of a classless society, calls for abolishing the Senate, the presidency and the Supreme Court. This is literally a revolutionary program to topple the American system as we have known it since 1789. It’s the kind of thing you might expect after angry rebels mount the barricades in Washington, D.C., and overthrow the government. It makes proposals to abolish the filibuster seem trifling in comparison and even makes court-packing look relatively moderate. The proposal to kill off the world’s greatest deliberative body has gotten the most attention. New York City’s DSA co-chair, Gustavo Gordillo, went on Fox News to explain that the senate is “undemocratic,” while Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has said that she opposes the filibuster and elements of the Senate that “were founded on Jim Crow.” Contrary to Gordillo, the Senate is a democratic institution; no one wins a Senate seat without getting more votes than his or her opponent. Yet, part of its role in our system is to serve as a check on popular passions. At the institution’s inception, state legislatures appointed senators. Those days are long gone -- the 17th Amendment, ratified in 1913, requires direct election -- but six-year terms and staggered elections give the Senate more insulation from the transient currents of public sentiment than the House of Representatives. Then there are the senate rules that put an emphasis on consensus and delay. AOC sounded confused when she cited Senate practices created under Jim Crow, the system of formalized racial discrimination that arose about 100 years after the creation of the Senate. It’s true that the filibuster was used as a tool to attempt to block landmark civil rights legislation, without ultimate success. But the filibuster is an instrument of every minority party in the Senate trying to block the agenda of a president of the opposing party, very much including Senate Democrats arrayed against President Trump today. The Senate has another function, which is giving small states equal representation with large states. This is the source of the charge that it is undemocratic. Why should Wyoming, population roughly 600,000, have as many senators as California, population nearly 40 million? This is meant, though, to keep large states from having overwhelming influence on the nation’s governance, and to give easy-to-ignore places a say in the nation’s affairs. For proportional representation, there’s the House; California has 52 members of Congress, whereas Wyoming has one. All this said, regardless of the merits, the Constitution deems the provision of equal senators for the states un-amendable: “No State, without its Consent, shall be deprived of its equal Suffrage in the Senate.” This suggests that the dissolution of the constitutional system couldn’t be achieved by constitutional means, since the Founders didn’t supply a readily available self-destruct button for their brilliant handiwork. Not that the DSA cares. What they are seeking would, in some ways, be a return to the Articles of Confederation, under which we had a unicameral legislature and neither a presidency nor federal courts. But this made for a very weak central government, while the DSA wants an overweening Washington, D.C., shorn of the inherent checks on the popular will that come with a multi-layered federal system. In short, it hopes for what Lord Hailsham, in his criticism of the British parliamentary system, famously called an “elective dictatorship.” Secretary of State Marco Rubio gave a speech last week in which he inveighed against left-wing extremists who seek to destroy rather than build, targeting “the physical embodied symbols of power and invention and achievement.” He might have added to the target list, with a nod to the DSA, the U.S. constitutional order; the socialists have met the enemy — and it is our own longstanding, highly successful governing institutions. 249 W. title: Beatrice V. Frederick 1942-2026 - Tribune Chronicle -
content: WARREN -- Beatrice Vada Frederick, of Warren, daughter of Ralph Morgan Perry and Laverne Katherine Stein Perry, passed away peacefully on Monday, July 20, 2026, at McCall Hospice House in Simpsonville, South Carolina. Beattie was married to Adam J. Frederick Sr. for 61 years. She was a homemaker, staying home while her children grew. She was a Sales Associate for over 25 years at Strouss/Kaufmans. She loved making quilts for loved ones as well. Beatie leaves her younger sister, Nora (Durwin) Loudin of Idaho. She will be missed greatly by her children, Christine (Steven) Smith of Simpsonville, South Carolina, Adam (Nanci) Frederick Jr. of Warren and Philip Frederick of Cortland. Grandchildren include Jessie Gravley, Joseph Acklin, Noah Smith, Jenna Frederick, Jordan Frederick, Hannah Bissonette, Hailey Hoberny, Summer Frederick, Jacob Frederick and Tristan Frederick. She also leaves 12 great-grandchildren, whom she loved so much. A private memorial service is planned for later in the year with family. title: Canon Adds Flash Support to the R6 V With New Firmware - PetaPixel
content: Canon Adds Flash Support to the R6 V With New Firmware Canon released new firmware updates for the EOS R6 Mark III and EOS R6 V cameras this week. Arguably the biggest addition of all is the ability to shoot with flash on the R6 V. While the Canon EOS R6 V is undoubtedly better suited to video than photography, the camera does have many of the same still photography capabilities as the R6 III, albeit without that camera’s mechanical shutter. It was this lack of a shutter that presumably led to the R6 V shipping a couple of months ago without the ability to use flash. The R6 III, for example, is not compatible with flash when set to its electronic shutter option. For that matter, the R6 V is still very limited with flash. Although Canon doesn’t offer specifics on its R6 V firmware page, DPReview notes that flash on the R6 V is limited to a maximum sync speed of just 1/60s, which is very slow. It is also worth recalling that the R6 V lacks a traditional five-pin hotshoe. It works with Canon’s Multi-Interface-equipped Speedlite units, but not traditional flashes. Nonetheless, it’s nice to have the option to use flash on the R6 V, as that was a rather notable omission for hybrid shooters. Other improvements introduced in firmware 1.1.0 include support for Canon’s new BR-E2 Wireless Remote Controller, support for Canon’s SDK, bug fixes, and improved “operational stability,” the most popular update in firmware history. The Canon EOS R6 III is also now at version 1.1.0. Compatibility with the BR-E2 has been added, and Canon has introduced SDK support for the R6 III, too. Canon has also added the option to set autofocus for close-up demos to the camera’s menus and the option to set a grid display during movie recording, features that were already available in the R6 V. Canon also addressed some potentially frustrating bugs, like FTP errors, an issue with interval shooting, and a USB problem. And, as always, operational stability is better now. Firmware 1.1.0 for the Canon EOS R6 V and the EOS R6 III is available to download now. title: 2026 Aston Martin Vanquish 25 First Look: A Silver Anniversary of V-12 Power - MotorTrend
content:
Available as a coupe or Volante convertible, the Vanquish 25 celebrates 25 years of Aston Martin’s flagship. Twenty-five years is a long time for a nameplate to stick around, especially one created in the early 21st century. But the Aston Martin Vanquish has indeed reached that silver anniversary, a milestone being marked with a special model available as either a coupe or convertible. Production will be limited to just 50 examples—25 of each body style—and feature bespoke details and paintwork created by Q, Aston Martin’s in-house customization house. The brilliant silver coating the cars is called Q Skye Silver, an exclusive paint developed just for the Vanquish 25. It shines brightly under the sun but takes on a much darker tone in the shadows. This contrast helps accentuate the car’s sculptural body lines. The Vanquish 25 also gets special side sills and metal-foil accents that include on the Aston Martin wordmark on the rear of the car. Stainless steel side strakes, unique exhaust tips, Vanquish 25 badging, and exclusive 21-inch wheels complete the exterior. Inside, the cabin of the Vanquish 25 features unique perforation patterns and split finishes. The headrests have embroidered Vanquish 25 logos and the Aston Martin wordmark is laser-etched into the trim. The bright red start/stop button is surrounded by unique trim, and black Alcantara lines the roof above occupants in both 2+2 and true two-seater configurations. Of course, the star of the show, and what makes the Vanquish special, is its Aston Martin V-12 engine. Under the hood of the 2026 Vanquish 25 sits the latest version of the 5.2-liter twin-turbo V-12, the AE31. Although this engine first debuted in the DB11 in 2016, enhancements made in 2024 for the current Vanquish’s debut strengthened the block, improved turbocharger response, and raised output to 824 horsepower and 738 lb-ft of torque. With that much power on tap, the Vanquish coupe is capable of a 0–60 mph time of 3.3 seconds and an 11.2-second quarter-mile at 132.5 mph in MotorTrend testing, as well as a top speed of 214 mph. The 2026 Aston Martin Vanquish 25 is set to make its physical debut during Monterey Car Week next month. Deliveries are scheduled to begin toward the end of this year. title: C.H. Robinson to appeal $604M verdict in Lipe v. Lupus Superior - Transport Topics
content: [Stay on top of transportation news: Get TTNews in your inbox.] Freight brokerage giant C.H. Robinson is appealing a $604 million jury verdict handed down July 24 in a case that found it liable for a 2021 fatal crash in Mississippi. The outcome of Lipe v. Lupus Superior comes less than three months after a landmark Supreme Court ruling affirmed that negligent hiring claims against freight brokers can proceed under state law. PREMIUM: Small brokers and carriers face pressure after SCOTUS ruling The case, tried in Dallas County Court in Texas, centered on whether C.H. Robinson and motor carrier Lupus Superior were liable for negligence relating to a crash that killed three people and injured two others. “We extend our deepest sympathies to everyone affected by this tragic accident,” Dorothy Capers, chief legal officer at C.H. Robinson, told Transport Topics. “Every loss of life on our nation’s highways is one too many. We strongly disagree with the verdict in Lipe v. Lupus Superior, LLC, et al. and will immediately appeal.” C.H. Robinson asserts that it should not be held liable and did not act negligently. The company pointed out that the carrier had safely delivered nearly 270 loads for its customers and held a satisfactory rating from the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration when it was selected. “Safety is core to how we operate and always has been,” Capers said. “We go beyond federal requirements and apply multiple layers of safety and risk criteria that we continuously re-evaluate and strengthen. The shipments we arrange overwhelmingly move without incident, with one serious accident claim filed for every 500 million miles driven on our customers’ loads.” Capers views the decision as reinforcing ongoing calls for the federal government to better address road safety. She also noted that the carrier maintained a satisfactory rating even after a federal review of the accident. C.H. Robinson, she pointed out, does not employ drivers. “The extreme nature of this verdict means it is even more imperative that Congress and the federal government act with urgency to establish clear and proper accountabilities across the transportation industry that enhance highway safety and support the uninterrupted flow of goods across the United States,” Capers said. Jennifer Lipe, Benjamin Brewer and Rhoderick Coleman burned to death in their vehicles after a Lupus Superior truck crashed into stopped traffic in Mississippi. Rodney Hawkins and Gabrielle Broussard were injured. The plaintiffs in the case were represented by law firm Arnold & Itkin. The largest 3PLs in North America continued to face volatile business conditions last year, from compressed margins to tariff-driven supply chain upheaval. Read more “No amount of money will replace the parents and spouses who burned to death in this horrible crash,” said Roland Christensen, attorney at Arnold & Itkin. “But this verdict is a message to C.H. Robinson and the brokering industry that their dangerous practices are not acceptable.” Christensen claimed the company refused to accept responsibility for hiring a motor carrier with a history of safety alerts. C.H. Robinson also was at the center of the Supreme Court’s Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II ruling, issued May 14. RELATED: C.H. Robinson sees clarity in Montgomery decision That case challenged whether federal law that restricts states from regulating brokerage services protects freight brokers from state lawsuits over negligent hirings. The high court’s decision is notable for undoing what had been a presumed protection for brokers. C.H. Robinson expressed optimism at the time that the ruling would lead to needed legal clarity. C.H. Robinson ranks No. 2 on the Transport Topics Top 100 list of the largest logistics companies in North America.

title: Aion V review — plush, yes … so why do I feel so uncomfortable? - The Times
content:
Would you buy a Chinese car? Have you already? There are arguably many reasons to be cautious before doing so. At the most basic level, the same concerns that would be true of any newcomer to the market are there: will the company survive over the difficult first few years and be able to provide after-sales support? If the car is involved in an accident, are there enough repair centres and spare parts available to get it fixed? But with Chinese brands the worries may be deeper. The Ministry of Defence is concerned enough about China using cars for espionage, using the onboard microphones and cameras that are increasingly common in cabins, that it has warned officials not to discuss sensitive information while inside any civilian vehicles. This is true not just of the state-owned carmakers, such as SAIC, which owns MG; Dongfeng, which manufactures the Dacia Spring; and Changan, which has a joint venture with Mazda to produce the new Mazda 6e. Even private firms such as BYD would have to hand over data to the Chinese state if they were asked for it, so the MoD casts them all in the same light. So even though about 165 BYDs are on the MoD fleet, alongside 1,376 MGs and another 198 from SAIC-owned Maxus, they are all treated the same. Why the MoD uses them at all is an excellent question. Apparently they are considered part of a “white fleet” that is “for routine business, not sensitive military activity”. You can bet affordability had a part to play, though — one imagines our government got an excellent deal on them. The companies involved insist they meet all legal and regulatory obligations when handling data, though it may give private buyers such as yourselves pause for thought. While the MoD is cautious, I’m downright opposed. If I lived in China, just writing the five paragraphs above could result in a knock on my door and the possibility of being re-educated, or “disappeared”. Journalists have been punished for less. And let’s not forget that human rights abuses in China are well documented by the likes of Amnesty International. Call me a stickler, but I’m not too keen on supporting companies either owned by or linked to authoritarian regimes that don’t take kindly to being held to account. Some people compare China’s entry into the UK market to when Japanese carmakers did the same thing in the 1960s and 1970s, but it’s not the same thing at all. China is more like its allies Russia or North Korea, and I’d not buy cars made by their manufacturers either. There are issues, too, if you want to talk about it in strict business terms, because it has not been a level playing field: the Chinese state has broken WTO rules according to many experts, including the former Conservative Party leader Iain Duncan Smith, and artificially propped up its businesses in order to dominate global markets. They were also smart in insisting on joint ventures with western carmakers in return for access to its own market, which was a money-spinner for the likes of Volkswagen, General Motors and Ford for about twenty years, but one might argue China’s scant regard for intellectual property is the reason its own cars are now competitive. All of which upsets my British sense of fair play. But taking the moral high ground is tricky when the Chinese carmakers are churning out objectively excellent products at bargain prices. The Aion V (“ay-on vee”) that you see here is a good example. Aion is owned by GAC Group, which is controlled by the regional government in Guangzhou, and although GAC is a newbie to the UK it has been producing vehicles under contract for other firms in China for decades, so it knows how to build a car. That experience means Aion isn’t turning up with a product that is shoddily made — one look at the panel gaps will tell you that, and the cabin exudes quality everywhere you look and touch. For example, the picnic table in the rear (available with the Premium pack) — there’s just one, fitted behind the passenger seat, the idea being that you can slide the front seat forward and work or watch a film on your laptop with plenty of legroom without changing the driving seat position — is not a flimsy flip-up job that you might find in a Renault or Fiat of old; it has a lovely, metal-bracketed hinge and folding action that the likes of Bentley would not be too ashamed of fitting to its cars. It’s genuinely impressive. The rest of the cabin is top notch too. Easily a match for western carmakers at the lower end of the premium market, with comfortable seats, quilted leather door liners, chrome-effect window switches and speaker covers, and a general sense that a good deal of work has gone into the details. OK, it’s laid out remarkably like a number of other new electric cars (I talked about that in my review of the Mazda 6e), and it could do with more physical controls, but there are no issues with quality. Aion’s quality control means the V is No 1 in the JD Power list for its class in China, so we can expect a good level of reliability and durability. In the UK customers are offered Aion’s “Great 8” package, which includes eight years’ warranty, roadside assistance, MoTs and servicing. I only had it for a week but drove from London to Liverpool and back and it didn’t skip a beat. I also felt comfortable making that journey as the advertised range from the 75.3kWh battery is 317 miles per charge, with a rapid charge from 10-80 per cent possible in 24 minutes, assuming you can draw the maximum 180kW. Because I was hammering it on mostly motorway and blasting the air-con, I saw 2.1 miles per kWh, which means the need to plug in at least every 158 miles, but that still meant I only needed to stop once each way. I’d make a joke about them being welcome breaks in every sense, because the Aion V is not the most pleasant car to drive, but actually it’s not awful on the motorway. I followed a Geely EX5 for a while, and noticed it had similar body control to my car — that is to say, neither had much of it at all, with both floating up and down over the undulations in the road. Being overtaken by a BMW 2 Series really highlighted the difference between a properly set-up suspension system and our cars — the Beemer glided along flatly with beautiful poise by comparison. On a twisty road, again the Aion will be fine for most drivers, but those who like predictability and a dynamic edge will be left wanting, because the steering is vague and the brakes inconsistent in feel. Apparently GAC employs 6,000 people at its R&D centre, and the Aion V’s chassis has been set up on UK roads, but some more work needs to be done to match more established rivals. Combine that with nannying driver aids, and the extreme level of intervention from the likes of the lane-keeping assist (there’s a Tesla-level semi-autonomous system with lane-change assist) and driver monitoring system, and it feels like the car is fighting you at times, rather than working with you. You need to go through the touchscreen to turn it all off, which isn’t easy when the infotainment screen is picking up reflections from the sun while travelling up the M6, I found. I try extremely hard to leave my preconceptions and biases at my front door when testing cars, but while there is plenty to like about the Aion V, I did think to myself while behind the wheel, am I not liking this simply because it’s a Chinese car? In the end I decided that, no, it’s objectively not as fun to drive as the competition. But if the company can bring its chassis up to the same standard as its interiors, the likes of Volkswagen, Kia, Skoda, Hyundai and Ford — and even Audi, BMW and Mercedes — are in real trouble. title: Barbara V. Worrilow Obituary Jul 24, 2026 - Crouch Funeral Home
content:
Barbara V. Worrilow, of North East, Maryland, passed away peacefully on Friday, July 24, 2026, at AccentCare Hospice at Christiana Hospital. She was 83. Born on March 25, 1943, in Virginia, Barbara was the beloved daughter of the late Alfred W. Cloud, Sr. and Juana M. Cloud. Barbara dedicated many years of her career to MBNA before retiring. Earlier in life, she proudly served as secretary to Sheriff Jack DeWitt. While she found fulfillment in her work, it was the simple joys of life that truly brought her happiness. She had a remarkable gift for creating beautiful things, whether through sewing, cake decorating, painting, or crafting. Barbara's creativity was matched only by her generous heart. She expressed her love through the thoughtful gifts she made, the time she shared with others, and the kindness she showed to family and friends. She will be remembered for her gentle spirit, caring nature, and the warmth she brought into the lives of those who knew and loved her. Barbara was preceded in death by her beloved husband, Raymond R. Worrilow, who passed away on October 18, 2019; her cherished son, Raymond R. Worrilow, Jr.; and her sister, Debra Cloud Leight. She leaves behind a loving family who will forever treasure her memory, including her son, Brian G. Worrilow and his wife, Laura, of Elkton, Maryland; her grandsons, Nathaniel G. Worrilow and Petty Officer Second Class (MA2) Joshua E. Worrilow, United States Navy, currently stationed at Naval Base Kitsap, Washington; her sister, Dawn Blackburn; her brothers, Alfred "Al" Cloud, Jr and James Wilkerson.; as well as many extended family members and dear friends who will miss her greatly.
